title: DNA Study Reveals a Third Ancestral Group Shaped Modern Japan
summary: A landmark genetic study has upended the traditional dual-origin model of Japanese ancestry. Researchers at RIKEN's Center for Integrative Medical Sciences analyzed whole-genome sequences from over 3,200 individuals across seven regions, from Hokkaido to Okinawa. Their results, published in Science Advances, strongly support a "tripartite origins" theory, adding a third ancestral group tied to northeastern Asia and possibly the ancient Emishi people. The study revealed that Japan's population is far more genetically diverse than previously assumed. "The Japanese population isn't as genetically homogenous as everyone thinks," said Chikashi Terao, who led the study. Jomon ancestry was highest in Okinawa (28.5%) and lowest in western Japan (13.4%), which showed stronger genetic links to Han Chinese, reflecting migration waves between 250 and 794 CE. The newly identified Emishi-related ancestry was concentrated in the northeast. Using whole-genome sequencing—which provides roughly 3,000 times more data than older microarray methods—the team built the Japanese Encyclopedia of Whole-Genome/Exome Sequencing Library (JEWEL). They focused on rare genetic variants, which can act as markers for ancient population splits. The findings align with earlier ancient DNA studies from 2021 that first proposed a third migration during the Kofun period. This layered history suggests multiple waves of people entered Japan over centuries, each leaving a genetic imprint. The research also explored Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA segments that persist in modern Japanese, some linked to disease risk or adaptation. By illuminating fine-scale regional differences, the study not only rewrites Japan's deep past but also lays groundwork for personalized medicine.
why_it_matters: This study reveals that no population is as isolated or genetically uniform as it might seem — migration has shaped us all. For Japan, this deeper genetic knowledge could lead to better medical treatments tailored to regional genetic profiles and reshape national conversations about identity and heritage.

background_read: For decades, the mainstream model of Japanese origins held that the modern population descended from two main groups: the Jomon (hunter-gatherers who arrived in Japan over 14,000 years ago) and the Yayoi (migrants from the Korean Peninsula and China around 300 BCE to 250 CE). The Jomon ancestry is especially noticeable in the indigenous Ainu and people of Okinawa, who often show physical traits distinct from mainland Japanese.

The new study led by Chikashi Terao at RIKEN (Japan’s largest comprehensive research institution) used whole-genome sequencing of more than 3,200 individuals to show that a third component — likely linked to the Emishi people of northeastern Japan — entered during the Kofun period (300–538 CE). This aligns with ancient DNA findings from 2021 that first hinted at a tripartite model.

Whole-genome sequencing provides about 3,000 times more data than earlier microarray-based studies, allowing researchers to detect rare genetic variants that act as historical signposts. The regional differences are striking: Jomon ancestry peaks at 28.5% in Okinawa and drops to 13.4% in western Japan, which shows stronger affinity to Han Chinese, reflecting later waves of migration.
The study also examined traces of Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA that modern Japanese carry — segments linked to both disease risk and adaptation, opening avenues for personalized medicine.

OPEN QUESTION: How will this genetic map influence health care and historical understanding in Japan?

perspectives.description: The research enriches Japan’s history by adding a forgotten genetic layer and demonstrates the power of whole-genome data. It also opens the door for precision medicine, as doctors may one day use regional genetic patterns to predict disease risk and drug response more accurately.

Some may find the idea of a genetically diverse Japan unsettling, as a narrative of homogeneity has long been part of national self-image. There is also a risk that the data could be misused for political purposes or to reinforce regional stereotypes, and the high cost of whole-genome sequencing may limit how widely this knowledge benefits ordinary people.

This finding mirrors global genetic studies that show almost every population is a mosaic of ancient migrations. Japan’s three-layer model echoes what we see in Europe (hunter-gatherers, farmers, steppe herders) or India (Ancestral North and South Indians), suggesting that human history is rarely a simple tale of two groups.

The JEWEL database could become a national reference, similar to the UK Biobank. If researchers can link rare variants to specific diseases, Japan could develop screening programs that account for regional differences. Other Asian countries may follow suit, building their own whole-genome resources and revealing a far more interconnected human past than textbooks describe.
